auditScope: episodeSelection orders 1-10 in source checkout; read-only source audit
method: URLs listed as consulted were opened/read for the cited locator or as an explicitly limited extract. Search snippets, abstracts, TOCs, and non-opened texts are not represented as full-paper reading.

episodes.event: Constantine dies in 337; his sons succeed

sources.title: Eusebius, Life of Constantine IV.64
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read returned chapter 64 text: Eusebius says Constantine apportioned the imperial inheritance among his children; chapter frames death in Pentecost festival. Translation is Schaff-era English, not Greek apparatus.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Eusebius writes as an admiring Christian encomiast; personal and succession details are rhetorically shaped. The chapter's Pentecost dating should not substitute for a modern date conversion/source-critical chronology.
sources.supports: Death narrative; Eusebius explicitly claims an inheritance arrangement among Constantine's children.
sources.doesNotSupport: The cited chapter alone does not establish the exact legal succession, which sons controlled which territories, nor that Constantinople instantly became the uncontested sole capital.

sources.title: Oxford Classical Dictionary / standard late Roman chronology required for succession contrast
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Needs direct access/check in full dossier.
sources.supports: Nothing claimed from this entry in this audit.
sources.doesNotSupport: Do not treat exact territorial allocation as audited.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Death is reported at Nicomedia (modern İzmit), outside the Constantinople local map. It can be conveyed as a later dispatch. The campaign's geographic policy correctly avoids treating Constantinople as an already mature exclusive capital in 337; institutional centrality consolidated over time.
episodes.recommendation: Keep event as an attributed report. Narrow claim to Constantine's death and dynastic succession; independently source the sons' actual accessions/territorial distribution before stating it as fact. Current candidate phrasing 'heredan el imperio y la capital oriental' overstates Eusebius IV.64.

episodes.event: Council of Constantinople, 381; canon 3 and creed transmission

sources.type: primary conciliar text in translated edition
sources.title: First Council of Constantinople, canons; canon 3
sources.exactLocator: Canon 3; accompanying editorial note on creed transmission
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened the council page and checked canon 3 plus its editorial discussion of the creed; did not inspect manuscript witnesses or a critical edition. Canon text reads that Constantinople's bishop has honor after Rome because it is New Rome.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Modern compiled English translation/editorial page, not the acta manuscript tradition. Text of the creed is not preserved as a verbatim 381 council act in the same way as canon 3; creed's attestation at Chalcedon 451 matters.
sources.supports: A council traditionally dated 381 and canon 3's rank-of-honor rationale.
sources.doesNotSupport: No modern Catholic/Orthodox institutional division, papal or imperial jurisdiction over all sees, or an uncontested creed-text provenance at 381.

sources.title: Anthony Kaldellis, Two Romes: Rome and Constantinople in Late Antiquity, chapter 'Two Romes, Beacons of the Whole World'
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Abstract only; not the chapter/full book. It identifies the topic as canon 3 and New Rome.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Abstract is not evidence for detailed argument; full monograph needs consultation for interpretive claims.
sources.supports: A credible academic follow-up source exists for late-antique Roman framing.
sources.doesNotSupport: No claim here is based on unviewed chapter text.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Council is located in Constantinople, but precise building/map footprint is not established by the cited canon. Use a generic city/council setting. Do not collapse honorific precedence into later ecclesiastical jurisdiction.
episodes.recommendation: The file's caution is well-founded. Separate the creed's transmission/history from the attested conciliar canon and keep canon 3 narrowly about precedence in honor.

episodes.event: Theodosius I dies in Milan in 395; eastern and western courts continue under Arcadius and Honorius

sources.title: Geç Roma Tarih Yazımında 395 Yılı ve İmparatorluğun Birliği İdeolojisi [395 in Late Roman Historiography and the Ideology of Imperial Unity]
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Landing-page/index summary states 395 is generally treated in historiography as final division; full article text not extracted in this collection pass. This supports treating 'division' as a historiographical framing needing qualification, not as a direct decree.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Do not infer article's full argument from the abstract. The distinction between administrative division, dual court government, and legal unity needs full reading.
sources.supports: The historiographical label 'final division' is contested/interpretive and warrants careful phrasing.
sources.doesNotSupport: Exact date, place of death, succession, or any particular dispatch content.

sources.title: Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History V; Zosimus, New History IV; contemporary consular/chronicle evidence
sources.exactLocator: Not directly consulted for this audit
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: A proper event dossier should read a primary passage and modern specialist treatment; primary histories differ in political/religious perspective.
sources.supports: Not used as direct evidence in this audit.
sources.doesNotSupport: The Britannica overview cited in source JSON has not been checked here.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Theodosius died at Milan; that is an off-map event. Constantinople can receive news. Avoid implying a formal legal dissolution of a single empire on a single date or modern 'Byzantine/Eastern Roman vs Western Roman states' without attribution.
episodes.recommendation: Recast as a dispatch about two courts/successions after Theodosius's death, with the reporter explicitly calling this an evolving division of governance. Source the death/succession from primary chronicle plus scholarship before approving.

episodes.event: John Chrysostom's second expulsion from Constantinople, 404

sources.title: Palladius, Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom
sources.exactLocator: Chapter IX, 'Intrigues and Violence at Constantinople'; see also chapter X for departure/sequelae
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read targeted passages. Palladius narrates a court official and soldiers ejecting John; the work also includes a first-person letter attributed to John about arrest and night ship departure. This was a limited passage reading, not the full dialogue.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Palladius is a partisan defender of John and his circle; narrative rhetoric should be attributed. The second expulsion belongs to 404 chronology, but this locator itself does not state a precise calendar day. The original New Advent URL is unrelated Chrysostom homily material, not Palladius.
sources.supports: Armed/court-backed expulsion from the church/city and exile; local scene can be grounded in a hostile political-religious conflict, with narration attributed to Palladius.
sources.doesNotSupport: Neutral impartial description, private motivations, exact day, or an omniscient view of every household/city action.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Constantinople is the event setting; Palladius does not establish a precise building footprint suitable for a map. Do not render the first expulsion, the second expulsion, and later exile/death as one event.
episodes.recommendation: Correct the source URL to Tertullian Society's hosted translation and preserve partisan attribution. Candidate is supportable if the episode says which expulsion it depicts and avoids invented private dialogue.

episodes.event: Imperial regulation of public teaching in 425 (often anachronistically called founding a university)

sources.type: primary legal text in Latin transcription
sources.title: Codex Theodosianus 14.9.3
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened returned Latin transcription and read CTh 14.9.3 passage/dateline; it concerns public teaching at the Capitolium, regulating who may teach publicly and reserving privileges for appointed teachers. Direct LatinLibrary host was mirrored under an odd URL. No full critical apparatus consulted.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Latin text is an online transcription of the legal text, not a critical-edition apparatus; the exact modern institutional interpretation is scholarly inference.
sources.supports: Theodosius II and Valentinian III regulated an imperial auditorium/public teaching at the Capitolium and categories of appointed teachers.
sources.doesNotSupport: A modern university foundation in the modern sense, nor a claim that legal/literary education was created from nothing.

sources.title: Bibliotheca legum, University of Cologne, Codex Theodosianus overview
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read the accessible institutional overview: code promulgated Feb 438, effective 1 Jan 439; cites Matthews, Laying Down the Law (2000) for further study. This is about the Code rather than the school constitution, so only used for research direction/context.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Reference page is a concise overview, not article-length treatment.
sources.supports: No claim about the 425 auditorium beyond the source's identified scholarly bibliographic lead.
sources.doesNotSupport: Does not validate 'university founded'.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Constantinople is the legal dateline. 'Capitolium' is not a safely identified surviving campus footprint; no modern university campus map. A generic teaching venue is safer than naming a known archaeological building.
episodes.recommendation: Use wording 'regulation/organization of imperial public teaching' rather than 'Theodosius founds a university'; do not imply access was universal or the school resembled a modern university.

episodes.event: Council of Ephesus (431), initial session, deposition of Nestorius and rival assembly after John of Antioch's delayed arrival

sources.type: primary conciliar acts in translated edition
sources.title: Council of Ephesus, Session I and related acts
sources.exactLocator: Session I extracts, heading 'Before the arrival of the Papal Legates'; cross-check Fordham compilation section on opening and subsequent rival proceedings
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened New Advent Session I extract and Fordham's sourcebook text. Read opening-session framing and Fordham translated narrative about Cyril presiding and the separate Antiochene assembly; not the complete acta or manuscript tradition.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: The surviving acts are proceedings produced by participants/factions; the NPNF translation and Fordham hosting are editorial/compiled, not neutral transcripts. 'Cyril's faction' began before John of Antioch's group arrived; avoid depicting consensual unanimity. The council's ultimate reception and doctrinal labels developed over time.
sources.supports: Opening session at Ephesus before papal legates; Cyril presided over the initial proceedings; Nestorius was condemned/deposed in the initial party's proceedings; rival meeting followed when Antiochene delegation arrived.
sources.doesNotSupport: A peaceful unanimous council, modern 'Nestorian church' labels as direct 431 self-description, or the claim that all groups participated in one agreed session.

sources.title: Richard Price (trans.), The Council of Ephesus of 431: Documents and Proceedings
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read accessible book record and summary only, not full paid book/chapter. It indicates first official session on 22 June 431 in the church named for Mary and emphasizes subsequent reception of decrees.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Metadata/abstract only; do not represent as reading Price's translation or analysis.
sources.supports: Provides an authoritative modern critical-edition lead and date/venue check at abstract level.
sources.doesNotSupport: Detailed textual or factional interpretation beyond the abstract.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Ephesus
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read institutional site overview: ancient Ephesus occupied successive locations around the changing Kaystros estuary; councils of 431 and 449 are associated with the city; Church of Mary archaeological remains are noted.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Modern heritage description and site boundaries do not prove the precise 431 meeting-room footprint or reconstruct shoreline at a specific council day.
sources.supports: Ephesus as the correct city setting and a dynamic port landscape; Church of Mary as an important archaeological anchor.
sources.doesNotSupport: Precise council map footprint or movement of individual delegates.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: The city is Ephesus (near modern Selçuk), not Constantinople. A local Ephesus map is possible at broad ancient-city scale; coastline/harbor are diachronic because silting moved the shore. Church of Mary is an institutional/archaeological anchor, but don't overstate exact floorplan use without site plan/dating.
episodes.recommendation: Strong candidate if split-session structure is explicit and sourced. Attribute contested actions to the acts/parties; separate actual council proceedings from a later simplified doctrinal label.

episodes.event: Relics of John Chrysostom translated from Comana to Constantinople, 438

sources.type: primary ecclesiastical history in translated edition
sources.title: Socrates of Constantinople, Ecclesiastical History VII.45
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read chapter text. It identifies transfer from Comana to Constantinople on 27 January in Theodosius II's sixteenth consulship, equivalent to 438, and the reception/transfer of remains. Target passage only; not full history.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Socrates writes retrospectively as a fifth-century Christian church historian; this is not eyewitness reporting for Chrysostom's death in 407. Translation is older English.
sources.supports: The translation occurred in 438 from Comana to Constantinople; distinguishes transfer from John's exile/death.
sources.doesNotSupport: A 410 date, exact modern road route, or a detailed eyewitness description of all ceremony logistics.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Comana is remote from Constantinople, so departure is off-map/reported. The Constantinople reception can use a generic urban procession. Socrates identifies the destination ecclesiastically; avoid speculative route or precise staging locations absent corroboration.
episodes.recommendation: Keep 438 (not 410). Any procession play should be an attributed, bounded fictional logistics episode around a documented relic transfer, not a reenactment claiming exact route details.

episodes.event: Promulgation of the Codex Theodosianus in 438; entry into force in 439

sources.type: primary legal source in Latin transcription
sources.title: Theodosian Novella 1, De Theodosiani codicis auctoritate
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read the Latin text/index extract for Novella 1; Fordham candidate URL not opened in this pass. This is a transcription, not critical apparatus.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Need confirm passage against Mommsen-Meyer critical edition. Compiler's legal language is official promulgation, not proof that copies had already circulated everywhere or that reception was uniform.
sources.supports: Imperial authorization/promulgation in February 438.
sources.doesNotSupport: Entry into force as of 438, or uniform practical implementation across both halves of the empire.

sources.title: University of Cologne Bibliotheca legum, Codex Theodosianus overview
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read overview: promulgated February 438, effective 1 January 439; gives critical edition reference Mommsen/Meyer 1905 and Matthews 2000 bibliography.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Concise institutional summary; legal effects and regional reception require specialist reading.
sources.supports: Chronological distinction between promulgation 438 and taking effect 439.
sources.doesNotSupport: Specific delivery route/copying process or a gameplay map of the compilation process.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Imperial source and compilation are Constantinopolitan court administration, but no precise archive/scribe workshop footprint is supplied. 'Distributed record collation' is a modern mechanic metaphor; do not call it a documented contemporary operation.
episodes.recommendation: The existing date distinction is correct. Say the Code was promulgated in 438 and took effect 1 Jan 439. Source candidate Fordham remains unverified; legal claims should ultimately cite critical edition or verified direct translation.

episodes.event: Council of Chalcedon, 451; Christological definition and canon 28 are separate actions

sources.type: primary conciliar canon in translated edition
sources.title: Council of Chalcedon, canon 28 (resolution at session 16)
sources.exactLocator: Canon 28; compare council act/standard numbering as session 16 resolution
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read canon 28. It calls Constantinople New Rome, gives equal privileges while ranking it after Old Rome, and assigns specified ordination jurisdiction in Pontic, Asian, and Thracian dioceses. Not all acts read.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: English is a translated edition. Canon was contested: the papal legates opposed it and Leo I rejected it; its reception was not uncontested/universal. Canon 28 is distinct from the council's Christological Definition.
sources.supports: The stated rationale and bounded institutional provisions of canon 28.
sources.doesNotSupport: An absolute equivalence of every jurisdictional power, a modern East-West schism, or the claim that Christological definition and canon 28 were a single act.

sources.title: Richard Price, The Acts of the Council of Chalcedon; standard conciliar act edition
sources.exactLocator: Not directly consulted as an edition in this pass
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: A full dossier should compare the act's Greek/Latin text and papal correspondence; avoid treating old English compilation as critical apparatus.
sources.supports: Research lead only.
sources.doesNotSupport: No text-specific claim in this audit.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Chalcedon was across the Bosporus from Constantinople, in Bithynia/Asia Minor (near modern Kadıköy); the episode's across-strait setting fits. The council's exact session venue should be sourced separately; the current city map policy should not relocate its proceedings into Constantinople.
episodes.recommendation: Preserve the explicit distinction between Christological definition and canon 28. For local map play, make ferry/landing context fictional and geographically broad; do not assert a specific 451 harbor/landing road from the canon.

episodes.event: Leo I accession/proclamation and coronation, 7 February 457

sources.title: 'Late Imperial Coronation Ceremonies', Harvard Studies in Classical Philology 30 (1919), pp. 37–47
sources.exactLocator: Discussion of Leo I's inauguration/coronation at pp. 43–45 in web transcription
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Read returned discussion: Leo's inauguration is characterized as older military procedure; source argues patriarchal crowning came into coronation practice between 457 and 519 and distinguishes evidence. This is a 1919 article, not current consensus check.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Old scholarship and its framing of imperial/church alliance should be re-evaluated with recent work. The cited Brittanica candidate has not been opened in this pass.
sources.supports: 457 accession ceremony has important military/political elements; caution against projecting later imperial coronation rite backward.
sources.doesNotSupport: The claim that the patriarch definitively crowned Leo in the later Byzantine ritual form.

sources.title: Chronicon Paschale, entry for 457; Theophanes, AM 5949/5950; compare Constantine VII, De Ceremoniis (later retrospective description)
sources.exactLocator: Not directly consulted in this pass
sources.coverageActuallyRead: None. Search results show source tradition is divided: older accounts attribute crowning to Anatolius; later scholarship notes uncertainty and military setting. This lead must be opened before use.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Chronicon Paschale and Theophanes differ in detail; De Ceremoniis is tenth-century retrospective, not contemporaneous 457 eyewitness evidence.
sources.supports: No direct primary claim accepted here until exact passage is read.
sources.doesNotSupport: Do not write 'the patriarch crowns Leo' as settled fact based only on the candidate Britannica overview.

sources.title: De Imperatoribus Romanis, Leo I
sources.coverageActuallyRead: Search result says 7 Feb 457 was first known coronation involving patriarch, army, and Senate; page was not opened/fully read during this pass.
sources.biasOrDateUncertainty: Search-result extract only; source's underlying citations must be followed before reliance.
sources.supports: A useful specialist-reference lead for accession date and historiographical framing.
sources.doesNotSupport: No claim is treated as verified from an un-opened result.

episodes.placeAndAnachronisms: Episode is local to Constantinople/its Hebdomon military field in later accounts; do not place the action at a generic palace/cathedral without evidence. 'Patriarch participates' is materially stronger than 'proclaimed by military and senate'; evidence for the exact rite is uncertain.
episodes.recommendation: Hold the precise ceremony claim. Read primary accounts (Chronicon Paschale/Theophanes) and modern scholarship directly. Candidate title can remain as a selection label, but do not script a patriarchal crown ritual or exact route until corroborated.

crossEpisodeControls.coverageActuallyRead: Opened and read institutional description of successive settlement positions along the changing Kaystros estuary, port channel/harbor basin, Church of Mary remains, and council tradition.
crossEpisodeControls.use: Can support city identity, broad archaeological context, and warning that shoreline is diachronic; does not fix an exact 431 shoreline or council footprint.

crossEpisodeControls.exactLocator: Istanbul Ministry of Culture page, description of historic peninsula overlooking Bosphorus and Marmara
crossEpisodeControls.coverageActuallyRead: Institutional current-geography description opened in search results; modern topography only.
crossEpisodeControls.use: Broad strait/peninsula orientation; not an ancient shoreline, route, landing point, or archaeological control. Must use a historical atlas / archaeological gazetteer for production map placement.

generalLimits: This is source collection and claim audit, not architect approval, episode design approval, a complete bibliography, or proof of gameplay. No scene/dialogue has been fact-checked because no full scenes were in the inspected selection records. Full texts were read only at the specific locators stated above.
